item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—While the 2026 Major League Baseball postseason remains in play, the offseason has officially begun for the Los Angeles Dodgers after their anticlimactic series sweep at the hands of the National League champion Milwaukee Brewers.
After the conclusion of the 2026 Fall Classic, the Dodgers are set to have a total of nine free agents hit the open market, an increase from five last season.
While the list reads as nine, it is essentially eight, as veteran infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball after the Dodgers’ Game Four loss.
Free Agents
(9): Blake Treinen, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Alex Vesia, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Tarik Skubal
Blake Treinen
Veteran right-hander Blake Treinen’s season ended during the final week of September after a right shoulder setback that forced him off the Dodgers postseason roster.
Treinen returned to Los Angeles after his 2024 World Series heroics on a 2-year, $14 million contract, and now the 38-year-old will be without a home entering an offseason that may be the final season of his career.
Evan Phillips
Right-hander Evan Phillips missed all of 2025 and returned toward the middle of the 2026 regular season due to Tommy John surgery. However, in his games played, he was very effective, going 3-2 with a 3.46 ERA.
Still, Phillips will be entering his age 33 season and has already missed significant time due to right elbow/arm injuries, and with multiple pitchers in the pipeline, it’s not hard to see the Dodgers moving on.
Kris Bubic
Acquired at the trade deadline, left-hander Kris Bubic is likely to get a contract this Winter as a starter, since that was his primary role before injuries derailed his 2026 season.
Bubic was an All-Star in 2025 and, with a thin free-agent market, could land a nice contract from a team desperate for starting pitching.
Miguel Rojas
Shortly after the conclusion of Game Four of the NLCS, veteran utility infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball, bringing an end to his 13-year playing career.
Rojas is expected to remain with the Dodgers organization in a player devleopment/coaching role.
Kiké Hernández
October hero Kiké Hernández is hitting free agency yet again this Winter, and after a subpar performance in October, minus one huge home run off Chris Sale in the NLDS, not much is known about whether the Dodgers will try to run it back for another 1-year deal.
Overall, Hernández missed most of the season while recovering from elbow surgery and an oblique injury and hit 4 home runs in 90 at-bats while posting a below-average 82 OPS+.
The fan favorite will enter his age-36 season, likely ending his Dodgers tenure for the second time.
Alex Vesia
Arguably the biggest free agent from the Dodgers bullpen this Winter is left-hander Alex Vesia, who has likely pitched his way to a sizable multi-year contract that the Dodgers might not be inclined to match.
Vesia, 30, posted an elite 2.64 ERA and struck out 74 batters despite a below-average fastball velocity, but with backend pitching at a premium, his market is likely to be heavy.
Brusdar Graterol
Brusdar Graterol’s career has been defined by injuries, and that likely will force his time in Dodger Blue to come to an end this Winter.
Despite a 2.78 career ERA, the right-hander has pitched only 7.1 innings for the Dodgers since the 2024 regular season, missing the entire 2025 and 2026 seasons due to right shoulder surgery.
Eric Lauer
Like Bubic, left-hander Eric Lauer will enter the market as a starting pitcher, and after a second-half renaissance with the Dodgers, where he went 7-2 with a 4.50 ERA, he could be a dependable backend starter to eat innings for a variety of clubs.
Tarik Skubal
The consensus No. 1 free agent this Winter across baseball is two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is set to demand a massive multi-year contract that could go north of $400 million.
While the Dodgers will no doubt be involved, it’s hard to imagine them matching that while already having so many long-term deals tied up, especially in their starting rotation already.
Skubal is likely to sign before the MLB lockout on December 1st to maximize his contract, such as fellow Scott Boras client Corey Seager did after the 2021 season.

Cody Snavely has been the co-editor of DodgersBeat and full-time host of the Bleed Los Podcast since February 2023. He has also written for multiple websites, such as Dodgers Way, Dodgers Low-Down, and Dodgers Tailgate. item.content:encoded:
LOS ÁNGELES - La temporada baja ha llegado antes de lo previsto para los Dodgers.
Antes de haber asimilado por completo la derrota del jueves por la noche (6-4) ante los Cerveceros en el Juego 4 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional —resultado que puso fin a su temporada y a su intento de lograr un tercer título consecutivo—, los Dodgers tuvieron que afrontar la realidad de que probablemente se avecinan cambios en el equipo.
Los Dodgers perderán a nueve jugadores debido a la agencia libre, un grupo encabezado por la figura más destacada del mercado, Tarik Skubal. Los otros jugadores que pronto serán agentes libres son el venezolano Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Evan Phillips, Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen, Eric Lauer, Kris Bubic y el venezolano Brusdar Graterol.
Gran parte del núcleo del equipo de Los Ángeles permanecerá intacto en el futuro previsible, por lo que la ventana competitiva no se está cerrando; sin embargo, este podría ser un periodo de transición entre una era del béisbol de los Dodgers y otra.
"Nunca puedes pensar que este es el final", dijo Rojas, quien permanecerá en la organización desempeñando un papel en el desarrollo de jugadores. "Y conozco muy bien a esta organización; no se conformarán con esta derrota".
A lo largo de 14 participaciones consecutivas en la postemporada, los Dodgers han encontrado formas fluidas de incorporar talento joven a sus plantillas para complementar a su núcleo de veteranos experimentados. Ese proceso ya ha comenzado con el dominicano Josue De Paula —el prospecto número 4 a nivel general según MLB Pipeline—, así como con el receptor suplente Dalton Rushing y el jugador de cuadro Alex Freeland.
No obstante, es posible que los Dodgers deban adoptar un enfoque más deliberado para asignar roles más destacados a sus jugadores jóvenes de cara al futuro, lo que dará lugar a decisiones interesantes durante esta temporada baja.
"No conocemos el futuro", comentó el dominicano Teóscar Hernández. "Pero algo que sabemos es que nos preocupamos los unos por los otros, nos cuidamos mutuamente y nos apoyamos durante todo el año... Este grupo es realmente especial, no por lo que hemos logrado en los últimos dos años y en este, sino simplemente por la unión que tenemos".
A continuación, un vistazo a algunas de las decisiones más importantes sobre el roster que deberán tomar los Dodgers durante esta temporada baja:
¿Participarán en la puja por Skubal?
Los Dodgers se desprendieron de dos prospectos clasificados entre los 100 mejores —el abridor listo para las Grandes Ligas River Ryan y el jardinero Zyhir Hope—, además del lanzador derecho Brady Smith, a cambio de contar con Skubal por un periodo de hasta tres meses. No fueron el único equipo dispuesto a hacer una gran inversión por un talento del calibre de Skubal, y lo mismo ocurrirá cuando este llegue al mercado de agentes libres por primera vez.
Skubal ganó su caso de arbitraje salarial contra los Tigres la temporada baja pasada, obteniendo un salario récord de US$32 millones. Se espera ampliamente que consiga la mayor cantidad de dinero garantizado jamás otorgada a un lanzador en la agencia libre, superando el contrato de 12 años y US$325 millones de Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
En su año previo a la agencia libre, Skubal se perdió seis semanas tras someterse a una cirugía en el codo izquierdo, pero aun así completó otra campaña sólida, registrando una marca de 12-7 y una efectividad de 2.72 en 26 aperturas con los Tigres y los Dodgers. Prefirió no hablar sobre su futuro inmediatamente después de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional (SCLN).
"Sí, realmente no voy a hacer comentarios sobre mi futuro", dijo Skubal. "El día de hoy es una porquería, ya sabes, y en eso es en lo que estoy pensando ahora mismo".
Aun así, Skubal expresó su agradecimiento por el tiempo que pasó con los Dodgers.
"Una organización increíble, compañeros increíbles, una afición increíble", dijo. "Es un honor llevar las letras 'L.A.' en el pecho y en la gorra".
¿Cómo le darán tiempo de juego para De Paula?
En septiembre, De Paula hizo que el salto de Doble-A a las Grandes Ligas pareciera sencillo, impresionando tanto a los Dodgers que logró entrar en el roster de postemporada como opción de bateador emergente. Sin embargo, su limitación radicaba en que el equipo de Grandes Ligas lo veía únicamente como bateador designado, una posición ocupada por Shohei Ohtani.
"Creo que la mejora que Josue mostró en los jardines entre 2025 y 2026 es real", comentó el mes pasado Andrew Friedman, presidente de operaciones de béisbol. "Y para nosotros, se trata de dar otro gran paso de cara a 2027. Él tiene las herramientas y la capacidad para lograrlo".
Con el tiempo, los Dodgers tendrán que poner a De Paula a jugar en los jardines. No obstante, sus jardineros titulares —Teóscar Hernández, el cubano Andy Pages y Kyle Tucker— tienen contrato vigente hasta la próxima temporada.
Si los Dodgers consideran que De Paula está listo para ser jugador titular habitual, eso probablemente implicaría, como mínimo, limitar el tiempo de juego de Hernández. También podría darse una medida más drástica: buscar un equipo interesado en asumir la última temporada garantizada de su contrato de tres años y US$66 millones.
Otra opción sería que De Paula comenzara la temporada en Triple-A, donde podría trabajar en su defensa en un entorno de menor presión.
¿Qué jugadores veteranos clave regresarán?
Entre los agentes libres inminentes, algunas de las bajas más significativas en cuanto a liderazgo serían Kiké Hernández, Phillips, Vesia y Treinen. El bullpen ciertamente podría tener hueco para lanzadores de situaciones críticas como Phillips y Vesia, pero el encaje de Hernández entre los jugadores de posición no está tan claro.
Hernández, el propio "Mr. October" de los Dodgers, tuvo una temporada regular marcada por las lesiones. Tampoco estuvo a la altura de su habitual rendimiento en postemporada, conectando apenas un jonrón solitario en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional (SDLN) como único imparable. Es una figura importante en el vestuario y, aunque le encantaría volver a Los Ángeles, sabe que sus necesidades y las del equipo deben coincidir durante la agencia libre.
"Me encantaría intentarlo una vez más, tratar de ganar otro", dijo Hernández. "Pero realmente no sé qué va a pasar. Espero volver y, si no es así, espero poder jugar en un equipo ganador".

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — After their earliest postseason exit in three years, the Los Angeles Dodgers head into the offseason facing uncertainty over next year.
Shohei Ohtani was dogged by injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the second half and into the playoffs that rendered him ineffective at the plate. The two-way superstar also didn't pitch after the All-Star break.
Whether Ohtani needs offseason surgery remains to be seen, although he acknowledged it's possible after Thursday's loss to the Brewers that completed Milwaukee's sweep of the NL Championship Series. If he does, would the recovery bleed into the start of next season?
A potential MLB lockout is looming with the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1. Team owners have proposed a salary cap — something the sport has never had — and the players' union has adamantly rejected the idea.
A work stoppage would give Ohtani extra time to heal, although during such time the Dodgers would be cut off from communicating with any player, leaving Ohtani to rehab either from possible surgery or from his injuries on his own.
Communication between Ohtani and the team on his health during the season was “awesome,” Andrew Friedman, president of baseball operations, said last month, but he added: “The fully sharing exactly how he's feeling, maybe not so awesome.”
Ohtani said he plans to resume pitching next year, when he'll turn 33 in July. He's already had two Tommy John surgeries.
“What he’s doing is unprecedented, and it takes a real toll,” Friedman said. “And as you get older, I think us just being very dialed is going to be really important.”
Roster turnover is likely, even without big changes in MLB spending rules
The Dodgers had baseball's second-highest opening day payroll this year at $323.3 million, behind the New York Mets at $358.4 million. If a salary cap were to be imposed, the Dodgers' spending would be constrained when play resumes.
Some of the roster could look different next year, too, with nine players set to become free agents after the World Series, led by two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is expected to command a huge deal.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal from Detroit just before the trade deadline in August. The left-hander was 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 regular-season games for his new team. In the postseason, he was 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA and 14 Ks. Skubal didn't want to discuss his future Thursday, although he expressed enthusiasm for the organization, his teammates and the fans.
Advertisement
Other impending free agents are infielder Miguel Rojas, utility player Kiké Hernández, and relievers Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Blake Treinen and Alex Vesia.
As expected, Rojas announced his retirement Thursday, saying, “This is it, guys. That was my last game played.” He'll still be around, though, to work in a player development role.
Dodgers add a bit of youth with De Paula
The Dodgers got a glimpse of the future when they promoted Josue De Paula directly from Double-A to the majors in September. His energy and at-bats at designated hitter during Ohtani's stint on the injured list made an impression, and the 21-year-old was added to the postseason roster as a pinch-hitter.
The team will look to De Paula to further improve as an outfielder in 2027, although finding playing time for him will be challenging given the trio of veteran starters: Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker. De Paula is also blocked at DH by Ohtani.
“I think the experience he got being up here and watching what our guys do on a daily basis just helped connect some dots for him,” Friedman said. “And so, physically, he is capable of being a good corner outfielder, and we’re going to continue to tap into that.”
Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Ohtani, Tucker, Max Muncy and Will Smith will remain the Dodgers' veteran core. But some supporting players could be offloaded, like Kiké Hernández. Playing on a one-year deal, the 35-year-old was limited to 41 games while recovering from injuries and he didn't provide his usual postseason pop.
Manager Dave Roberts refused to blame an aging lineup for getting swept by the Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were three more than the Dodgers.
“We got beat,” he said. “There’s no because we’re too old or whatever. Every facet of the game, if you kind of unpack it, we were bested.”
There's drama off the field, too.
Owner Mark Walter was noticeably absent from the team's playoff games. He is facing multiple federal investigations into his business empire for possible financial improprieties involving insurance companies he controls. Walter has denied any wrongdoing. Since August, he sold his controlling interest in the Los Angeles Lakers and last month he unloaded his share in Chelsea of the Premier League.

item.content:encoded:
On Thursday, the Los Angeles Dodgers shockingly had their season come to an end when they were swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLCS.
They lost the final game by a score of 6-4 (at home) in Los Angeles.
Ex-Blue Jays Star To Become Free Agent
With their season now over, it’s worth noting that a former Toronto Blue Jays star will become a free agent this winter.
Eric Lauer will be available to sign with any team in the MLB.
Lauer had been traded to the Dodgers (via the Blue Jays) during the middle of the 2026 season.
He finished the year going 8-7 with a 5.23 ERA in 22 games (18 starts).
That said, Lauer got hurt during the middle of the year (and has not pitched since September 1).
MLB.com wrote (on October 15): “Was ineligible to be activated from the IL before the end of the season and is set to become a free agent.”
Looking At Lauer’s Time In Toronto
Lauer spent part of two seasons in Toronto.
Despite struggling in 2026 (before the trade), he had been coming off an impressive 2025 season.
In addition to making the World Series that year, Lauer went 9-2 with a 3.18 ERA in 28 games (15 starts).
MLB.com wrote (on May 17): “Toronto Blue Jays traded LHP Eric Lauer to Los Angeles Dodgers for cash.”
Looking At His Other Stops
Lauer was picked in the 1st round of the 2016 MLB Draft.
He spent the first two seasons of his career with the San Diego Padres.
Following San Diego, Lauer had a four-year run with the Milwaukee Brewers.
His best season was with Toronto.
There is no question that the 31-year-old will be an intriguing free agent this winter.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers appeared poised to three-peat as World Series champions. They loaded up after winning their second straight title, signing Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz in free agency and trading for Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline. All they had to do was get through a Milwaukee Brewers team they swept in last year's NLCS in order to appear in a World Series against either Tampa Bay or Cleveland, both of whom L.A. would be favored to take care of.
Instead, the Dodgers' incredible run was stymied by Milwaukee in an NLCS that can only be classified as embarrassing for L.A. The Dodgers could not get anything going offensively, and their vaunted rotation underwhelmed. Now, with their three-peat bid having been a failure, an important offseason is ahead. Will Tarik Skubal be back? That shouldn't be ruled out. These other players, though, almost certainly won't be back with the Dodgers seeking revenge in 2027 (if there even is a 2027 season).
INF Miguel Rojas
Why not start out with an easy one? Miguel Rojas has made it clear that he plans on retiring after the 2026 campaign. He can always change his mind, and he told Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times that he wouldn't play for another team, but with Rojas now 37 years old and with a pair of World Series wins on his resume, what more does he have to play for?
Rojas retiring would be a tough blow for the Dodgers, given the fact that he's still a solid bench piece, is an important clubhouse presence, and recorded one of the biggest and unlikeliest hits in MLB history when he tied Game 7 of the 2025 World Series with a home run, but it's hard to imagine Rojas sticking around for another year.
RHP Blake Treinen
Once upon a time, Blake Treinen was one of the best relievers in the sport. He saved 38 games for the Athletics in 2018, and had a pair of sub-2.00 ERA seasons for the Dodgers in 2021 and 2024. Unfortunately, Treinen has a 4.47 ERA in 68 appearances since the start of the 2025 campaign, and injuries have limited him to fewer than 40 outings in each of those years.
Treinen missed nearly three months of the 2026 campaign with elbow inflammation, didn't pitch all that great upon his return, and was placed on the IL with shoulder inflammation at the end of the regular season. Injuries have been a common theme for Treinen over the course of his career, and while he had always been good enough to keep around despite his missed time, now, at 38 years old, he isn't what he once was. It's hard to envision the Dodgers being eager to bring him back.
LHP Kris Bubic
The Dodgers bolstered their pitching depth by acquiring Kris Bubic at the trade deadline from the Kansas City Royals. Sure, Bubic was hurt at the time, which made the move a bit risky, but L.A. made this move with the postseason in mind. Well, while Bubic came through with five scoreless appearances in the regular season, he allowed a run in each of his postseason appearances, taking a loss in the NLDS against the Braves and blowing a rare lead the Dodgers had in Game 2 of the NLCS against the Brewers.
These rough outings aren't reason enough to not want to bring Bubic back, but odds are, the southpaw is going to want to start (he was rock-solid in that role with the Royals), and I'm not sold that the Dodgers will be eager to guarantee him a rotation spot, with Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow locked in if healthy, and guys like Justin Wrobleski, Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan still in the organization. Odds are, Bubic will earn a solidified rotation spot elsewhere.
LHP Eric Lauer
The Dodgers dealt with a slew of pitching injuries, and brought Eric Lauer in to give them needed depth. To his credit, Lauer pitched quite well in his 13 appearances (11 starts) for the Dodgers. In fact, He allowed three earned runs or fewer in nine of his 11 starts and allowed just one run in eight innings in two appearances as a bulk reliever. If it weren't for a couple of especially brutal starts, Lauer's numbers in L.A. would've wound up looking much better than they did.
With that being said, Lauer ended the year on the IL with left elbow inflammation and, as is the case with Bubic, is probably looking for more of a solidified role than the Dodgers would be willing to give him. He'd be a solid option to bring back in a swingman role, but it's likely that the 31-year-old will end up elsewhere.
OF Teoscar Hernandez
Here's the big one. Teoscar Hernandez is the only player on this list under contract for 2027, and he's been a staple in L.A. since the 2024 campaign. There're a couple of reasons why it makes sense to move him, though. First, he's simply not worth the $17 million he's owed in 2027 after the year he just had. He still mashes left-handed pitching, but he had a subpar .695 OPS against righties in the regular season and is a very poor defensive outfielder. It's hard to justify playing him regularly on a team trying to contend.
Second, and perhaps most importantly, the Dodgers need to find a spot for top prospect Josue De Paula to play regularly. The ideal spot for De Paula, an outstanding hitter whose defense leaves much to be desired, would be DH, but that's Shohei Ohtani's spot for the foreseeable future. Kyle Tucker is locked into right field given his absurd contract, and De Paula can't play center field (nor should the Dodgers be eager to move off of Andy Pages). That leaves left field, Hernandez's spot, as the position where De Paula seems likeliest to slot in.
The Dodgers can keep Hernandez around as a platoon partner for De Paula, but a trade could make sense. Hernandez was in rumors last offseason, and I wouldn't be surprised to see those resurface this winter.

item.content:encoded:
The success of a dominant team over a lengthy period like the Dodgers' relies on an adaptability to work your way through multiple iterations of a roster. While in the postseason you can find success in different ways, one aspect of regular-season success is how you handle injuries, particularly for a team as cautious as the Dodgers.
A common theme in recent seasons has been the Dodgers' pitching staff overcoming all sorts of obstacles to consistently provide terrific numbers. Postseason baseball funnels everything, and meritocracy only takes you so far when the goal is to win short series, but that doesn't mean the impact of productive but unceremoniously overlooked starters shouldn't get the credit it rightfully deserves.
There are layers of this tier, and we're not here to discuss the Justin Wrobleskis of the world, who'll morph into a different but still impactful role because their talent level demands a presence on the postseason roster, one way or another. This is an article for the Eric Lauers — pitchers who served a very specific and much-needed purpose in the regular season, but whose eventual playoff showing would only come in garbage-time scenarios; in Lauer's case, not even that, given he has ended the season on the injured list.
When Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow went down this year, as they often do in the regular season, the Dodgers took to the market early in the season for a veteran steady presence. Lauer did more than just go out there with league-average production or so.
The former Brewer worked on some adjustments with the Dodgers' pitching staff and led the team to a win in each of his first nine starts, boasting an ERA under 3.00 through that period. It'd be no stretch to argue that, at the very least, this chase for a playoff bye would look a lot different with a ton more pressure had it not been for Lauer's timely production. His final line with the Dodgers looks far worse than he pitched due to a couple of blowups against NL Central teams (4.50 ERA in 12 games), but his impact through most of that period was undeniable.
Even in the best of moments for Lauer with the Dodgers prior to his season-ending injury, it was evident that he would not play a key role in the playoffs, but it was about doing a specific job. While he was the best example in this year's current squad, going back through the recent track record, the names pile up, and here we'll look at a few others that might stand out—who perhaps didn't receive the right amount of due at the time, and certainly not when playoff ball rolled around.
Prospects with potentially limited big-league upside
This season's starting pitching problems are a cakewalk in comparison with what this team had to deal with a year ago. On the lookout for starting pitching contributions for much of the 2025 campaign, the Dodgers saw Dustin May come full circle on a sped-up version of your traditional career, entering the innings-eater portion far earlier than anyone would've anticipated, one of three starters on the team to cover 100-plus innings, this despite getting dealt at the deadline.
May, more than probably any other pitcher on this list, really pushed the envelope of what we can consider helpful volume, even with the caveat of potential uncertainty on door number two. It's easy to be dismissive of his ERA in the high 4.00s that got progressively worse until the team dealt him when it got healthier in the second half—through the majority of those innings, though, it literally had no one else. And if we want to get a little cute about it, the health he displayed in that period certainly played a role in helping the Dodgers land the offer they sought, with James Tibbs III joining the fold. It's about finding advantages anywhere.
If May represents the low end of the expectation pool for a pitcher of his caliber receiving this type of role in a contending team, a year prior Gavin Stone showed the best-case scenario. On the way to their second World Series of this era, it was the youngster Stone who led the Dodgers in innings pitched that regular season, before injuries cut short his campaign and development, which has been affected until the present day.
Even before the injuries, it was becoming increasingly clear in the second half of that 2024 campaign that Stone's postseason role would diminish, particularly so after the Dodgers acquired Jack Flaherty at the deadline. The changeup-heavy approach with below-average strikeout numbers caused enough concern that he likely wouldn't have stuck in the rotation one way or another.
Both in very different places right now, one still in the organization, May and Stone were once regarded as highly touted pitching prospects. Although their development wasn't as smooth as the Dodgers would've liked, they showed up to provide support at times of need, and their contributions meant a lot in championship-winning seasons.
Former stars in unique spots
Clayton Kershaw gave his best years to the Dodgers when they weren't nearly at their best and did so with the utmost grace and power. After a second chapter of his career, still dominant but maybe not quite Kershaw-dominant, came to an end in 2023, he stuck around for a couple of more years and only then genuinely looked mortal, but still quite helpful.
Missing the bulk of the 2024 season recovering from shoulder surgery, Kershaw came back healthier for one final year in 2025, and while his All-Star nomination might've been a tad sentimental, the 11-2 record was eye-catching, with a productive 124 ERA+.
Sitting below 90 MPH on his heater, there were clear limitations to what Kershaw could provide, but not only did he appear on the postseason roster. But he also managed to get one immense out in the never-ending Game 3 of that year's World Series. The plan was never to have him play a big role in October, but circumstances gave him a memorable cameo.
Going back to the regular season contributions, Kershaw, alongside May, was one of three Dodgers starters to surpass 100 innings in 2025. On the subject of his impact on that 93-69 record, there was nothing sentimental about it; he thoroughly helped a team that relied on him far more than expected.
Going back a few more years, the Dodgers needed to take on the David Price contract in order for the Mookie Betts deal to go through with Boston. And although that was a bad deal, it didn't mean Price couldn't be of assistance.
Opting out of the 2020 campaign, Price came in 2021 ready to embrace whatever role the Dodgers had for him, and he delivered a 105 ERA+ in over 70 innings, moving back and forth between the rotation and the bullpen. While the rotation was healthier that year, it didn't mean his presence went unnoticed, one of the more heavily used arms navigating between the rotation and the bullpen.
The OGs of this role in this run
When you first started reading this article, there is a decent chance one of the first names that came to mind was Mitch White or, particularly, Ross Stripling — the latter personally thanked by Dave Roberts in the World Series-winning speech back in 2020, a year in which he was traded from the team that August.
Between 2016 and 2019, Stripling pitched nearly 400 innings of regular-season baseball with a 115 ERA+, moving around to whatever role fit the team best. Seeing them finally break through to win it all the year in which he was dealt (2020) quickly made Dave and many others remember all he had done for this team.
It's a shame that at his best in 2018, working primarily as a starter, Stripling saw his campaign cut short due to injury and couldn't be available in that postseason. In 2020, the Dodgers stuck with him as much as possible, but eventually cutting ties seemed like the only answer with an ERA well above 5.00 in a shortened campaign.
White is the ideal example to note how, in most of these cases, whether the Dodgers get these players late, early, or even develop them from the minors, they seem to shine brightest here. In three seasons with the Dodgers, White had a 116 ERA+ in a little over 100 innings. Not only did he fail to reach similar heights after leaving the team, but his exposure was very limited, covering just 79.1 innings in two seasons since. Out of the bigs since 2024.
Surely there were other names in recent memory that we might've skipped over. Let us know who your favorite regular-season starting pitcher contributor is, or even all-time. It's always a fun conversation to have with no right or wrong answer.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts did not mince his words when talking about Edwin Díaz during his mid-September rehab assignment. "He needs to pitch better. It hasn't been good," said Roberts.
Diaz, who has the highest average annual value in MLB relief pitcher history ($23M), struggled in the first four appearances of his rehab assignment. He had thrown just 40 of 86 pitches for strikes in his first four games with Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Diaz's fourth appearance was especially worrying. He threw 30 pitches — just 13 of them for strikes — walked three batters and allowed five runs. Diaz rehab came in the Pacific Coast League, which is notorious for being the most hitter-friendly league in all of baseball. That atrocious outing came in Sugar Land, however, which is the most pitcher-friendly venue in the PCL.
When the Dodgers activated Diaz from the injured list, Roberts revealed he'd be used in low-leverage situations. Well, he has been perfectly fine in his three low-leverage outings since September 18, which has assuaged some of the Dodgers fans panic levels.
Should Dodgers fans buy into Edwin Diaz’s success?
Diaz has only allowed one hit since returning from the IL. The Dodgers, however, had a run margin of +19 in those three games.
“The way he’s throwing, the ninth is possible, yes,” said Roberts after the Dodgers 7-0 win over the Padres on September 22.
The Dodgers will almost certainly give Diaz another opportunity against the San Diego Padres on Thursday. The current home series against the Friars will be Diaz's last opportunity to pitch against a playoff team before the postseason begins.
The Dodgers are currently without Emmet Sheehan, Edgardo Henriquez, Will Klein, and Eric Lauer. Outside of Alex Vesia, the rest of the bullpen is incredibly shaky. Tanner Scott has a 5.40 ERA so far this month, Justin Wrobleski has not improved since being moved to the bullpen, and who knows what Blake Treinen has left in the tank?
Dodgers fans should get accustomed to seeing Diaz the rest of the season. He's quite possibly the linchpin to this team going deep in the playoffs with the way this bullpen looks right now. Dodgers fans have the right to remain skeptical that Diaz will return to the optimal version of himself,
